1.pericope_label: The people gather weeping to Ezra; Shechaniah proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives

schools.summary: Henry has it noised abroad that their new governor, in whom they rejoiced, was himself in grief for them and their sin, so that a great congregation assembled to mingle their tears with his, and draws the rule that our weeping for other people’s sins may set those a weeping for themselves who would otherwise continue remorseless; when a man in authority under the king lamented the public corruptions so deeply, they concluded the corruptions were indeed grievous. On Shechaniah he agrees the man was not himself guilty, since had he had the beam in his own eye he could not have seen so clearly to pluck it out of his brother’s, and guesses that his father’s strange wife may have been an unkind step-mother who made mischief in the family — if so, not the only time private resentments have been overruled by providence to serve the public good. On the hope offered he asks where else there should be hope but in Israel, since strangers to that commonwealth are said to have none, and holds the case sad but not desperate, the disease threatening but not incurable, now that it is discovered half cured, the valley of trouble being the door of hope, for the sin that truly troubles us shall not ruin us. On the remedy he both urges it and refuses it as a precedent: what has been done amiss must be undone as far as possible, and sin must have a bill of divorce given it though it be dear as the wife of one’s bosom, yet Shechaniah’s counsel will not hold now, since marriages with unbelievers are sinful and ought not to be made but are not null, what ought not to have been done must being done abide, and the gospel rule is that a brother with an unbelieving wife pleased to dwell with him should not put her away.
Gill takes Shechaniah for one of those who had come up with Ezra from Babylon, and makes the hope conditional on repentance and reformation.

Keil and Delitzsch set out Shechaniah’s confession and proposal as one speech, and dissent from the common identification of his family, holding that the Jehiel named later in the chapter is not this man’s father and that this Shechaniah is a different person from the descendant of Zattu named earlier. They note that Ezra had remained upon his knees throughout the speech before rising to administer the oath.

Clarke reads the weeping as fear of a displeasure about to light on them, notes that Shechaniah speaks for the people without acknowledging himself culpable since his name is not in the list that follows, takes him for a chief man whose support Ezra needed, and glosses the word for hope as expectation of pardon. Wesley adds that the account of Ezra’s grief before the temple was dispersed over the city in an instant, and then repeats Henry’s own sentence about the happy influence the example of great ones may have upon their inferiors. He finds Shechaniah absent from the catalogue but his father Jehiel and five other sons of his grandfather Elam present in it, and makes that the measure of the man, that it was evidence of great courage to discharge his duty so freely, honouring God above his nearest relations; and on the remedy he attends to the children, cast out of the commonwealth of Israel but not utterly forsaken, provision being probably made for them by authority.

debates.question: Was Shechaniah himself implicated in the trespass?

positions.view: No — his name is absent from the list, though his father and uncles are in it, which is the measure of his courage
No — he could not have seen to pluck the mote from his brother’s eye with a beam in his own, though his father and his father’s house were guilty
The Jehiel named later is not his father at all, and this Shechaniah is distinct from the man named earlier

debates.question: Does Shechaniah’s remedy bind Christians in mixed marriages?

positions.view: No — such marriages are sinful but not null; the gospel rule is not to put away an unbelieving wife willing to stay
Does not raise the question, but notes the children were provided for rather than abandoned

outliers.claim: Alone in refusing to let Ezra’s divorce stand as a precedent, and in setting the gospel rule against Shechaniah’s counsel.
Alone in denying that the Jehiel named later in the chapter is Shechaniah’s father.
Alone in guessing that a resented step-mother may have sharpened Shechaniah’s zeal against the foreign marriages.

themes: when Ezra had prayed, and when he had confessed, weeping
we have trespassed against our God
yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing
let us make a covenant with our God

6.pericope_label: A proclamation under pain of forfeiture; the people assemble in the rain and a commission is asked for

schools.summary: Henry notes that Ezra, authorised by the king to enforce his orders with penalties, threatened forfeiture and outlawry, the doom of a man who would not attend being that his substance should in his stead be for ever appropriated to the service of their religion while he himself was for ever excluded from its privileges. On the rain he reads two things at once: it was a token of God’s displeasure, which perhaps kept some away and was grievous to those who met in the open street, yet when they wept the heavens wept too, signifying that though God was angry at their sin he was well pleased with their repentance, and it was besides an indication of that repentance’s good fruits, since rain makes the earth fruitful. On the commission he gives the reasons it could not be done on the spot — the thing was not yet put into a method, the people could not stand out in the rain, the delinquents were many and would take time to examine, and nice cases would arise that could not be adjudged without debate — and has them conclude that taking time they would have done the sooner, whereas doing it in a hurry they would do it by halves. He adds what he plainly admires, that Ezra let his zeal be guided by the people’s prudence and was not ashamed to own the advice came from them.

Gill accounts for the shortness of the notice, that three days was fixed for quick dispatch, to forestall any scheme to obstruct the business, and lest those who had agreed should repent and go from their word; and he reads the proposal of a commission as the settling of the great court of judicature at Jerusalem.

Keil and Delitzsch make the legal point exactly: the forfeiture is not destruction of the goods, as the law prescribed for a city fallen into idolatry, but their appropriation to the temple on the analogy of another statute. They put the need for a commission administratively, the cases being too many for one hearing, so that the rulers as judicial authorities must decide and the offenders in every city appear before them.

Clarke reaches the same reading of the forfeiture as Keil and Delitzsch and finds the Greek version already there, rendering it that all the man’s substance shall be devoted to a holy use, he himself excommunicated and exiled from Israel. He declines to read the rain as a sign at all and gives the season instead: the ninth month answers to part of our December, the coldest and most rainy part of the year in Palestine, and the Greek renders the clause simply because of the winter. He alone looks past the decision to what it cost and whether it held, calling the dismissal a great hardship on women and children who did not know the law that made such marriages void, refusing to have them turned away desolate since humanity must have dictated a portion for each according to her husband’s circumstances and no law of God is contrary to humanity, and raising the doubt whether they did put them finally away, since years later Nehemiah found Jews married to wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab. Wesley keeps only the displeasure in the rain, and reads the proposal as the settling of the great council with the local judges joined to it as best able to inform it of the persons and the facts.

debates.question: What does the great rain signify?

positions.view: Both displeasure and acceptance — when they wept the heavens wept too, and rain makes the earth fruitful
A token of God’s displeasure against them
Not a sign but a season — the ninth month is the coldest and rainiest in Palestine
There is room to doubt they put the wives finally away, since Nehemiah later found the same offence
Treats the commission as having carried the matter through

outliers.claim: Alone in doubting that the wives were finally put away, on the evidence of the same offence recurring under Nehemiah.
Alone in insisting the dismissed women must have been provided for, since no law of God is contrary to humanity.
Alone in reading the rain as a sign of acceptance as well as of displeasure.

themes: he did eat no bread, nor drink water
all his substance should be forfeited
trembling because of this matter, and for the great rain
ye have transgressed, and have taken strange wives
as thou hast said, so must we do

15.pericope_label: Two men named at the business, the commission seated for three months, and priests found among the guilty

schools.summary: Henry gives the employed sense of the two men first, guessing these were the men who had made the proposal and so the fittest to pursue it, but then reports Lightfoot’s contrary reading, grants the original will very well bear it, and adds that it would be strange if a work of this kind met with no opposition at all. On the commission he is admiring and precise: Ezra presided with chief men of the fathers qualified with wisdom and zeal above others, and it was happy for them to have such a man to head them, since they could not have done it well without his direction, though he would not do it without their concurrence; they began on the first day of the tenth month, ten days after the method was proposed, and finished in three, and must have sat closely to despatch so many causes in the time. He adds the qualification that makes the delay intelligible, that everyone impeached was presumably asked what cause he could show against being parted, and that, judging by other cases, a wife proselyted to the Jewish religion was not to be put away — a trial requiring great care. On the priests he notes that many, and even of the high priest’s family, were found in the trespass though the law had particularly provided for the honour of their marriages; those who should have taught others the law broke it themselves and by their example emboldened others. On the binding he has them promise under their hand, reports that some think the oath was made with hands lifted up, and names the law behind the ram as the offering appointed for a trespass, so that in bringing it they owned both their guilt and its desert.

Gill takes the two men as employed, to see the affair conducted as proposed, each city’s magistrates bringing the delinquents in turn. On the priests he makes the inference the other way about from Henry’s: it need not be wondered at that the evil spread among the people when those who understood the law, and should have taught it, set such an example.

Keil and Delitzsch take the contrary sense of the two men, that they opposed the proposal and were backed by two Levites without being able to carry it; they read the opening particle as a qualification of the assembly’s agreement, cite Lightfoot and a rabbinic authority for the construction, and set against them the Vulgate and one explanation they call decidedly incorrect, noting that nothing further is known of the four. They supply the genealogy of the guilty priests, that the four named first were sons and brethren of the high priest Jeshua and, by the earlier roll, distant cousins of his; and they take the giving of hands literally, as binding themselves by a handshake to dismiss the wives and sever them from the congregation, the following word condemning them to bring a ram for their trespass.

Wesley reads the two men as employed and fills out the office, that they were to see each city’s officers and offenders come in order, keep account of the names dispatched, and prepare the business for the judges, making these two priests and their helpers Levites so that they might inform the parties in any matter of doubt; and he notes that the commissioners sequestered themselves from all other business and gave themselves wholly to this. Clarke counts the same three whole months of examining and separating, and has the priests bind themselves in the most solemn manner as the other delinquents had, acknowledging their iniquity by each offering a ram.

debates.question: Were Jonathan and Jahaziah employed in the business or opposed to it?

positions.view: Employed, to see it conducted as proposed
Opposed, with two Levites backing them, on the force of the opening particle; Lightfoot and a rabbinic authority agree
Gives the employed sense but reports Lightfoot’s contrary reading and grants the Hebrew will bear it

debates.question: What does giving their hands mean?

positions.view: Binding themselves by a handshake
Promising under their hand, though some think the oath was made with hands lifted up
Binding themselves in the most solemn manner, as the other delinquents had

outliers.claim: Alone in noting that a wife proselyted to the Jewish religion was not to be put away, which explains why the hearings took three months.
Alone in praising Ezra for letting his zeal be guided by the people’s prudence and owning that the advice came from them.
Alone in weighing the Vulgate against Lightfoot on the two men, and in calling one modern construction decidedly incorrect.

24.pericope_label: The singers and porters close the clerical roll, and the laity’s list begins

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch count one singer and three porters here, bringing the Levites to ten in all, and refer both orders back to the roll of those who had returned from exile where the same classes are enumerated. They read the phrase that follows as the heading of a new class, of Israel meaning the laity as distinguished from priests and Levites, and count eighty-six names in it belonging to ten families of those who returned with Zerubbabel, each identified against their own survey of those families, with one name they would read differently on the authority of the written text against the vowels supplied for it. They alone treat the roll as a damaged document: the sons of Bani are named twice over in the one list, which they call strange and judge a copyist’s error rather than a fact, so that one of the two headings must stand for another family, Bertheau conjecturing that a different name had once stood there. They locate the fault in the second occurrence and argue it from the arithmetic rather than the spelling, since every other family contributes four, six, seven or eight men while no fewer than twenty-seven names follow the second heading — too many for one family, so that a whole block of names has been gathered under a heading not belonging to them.

Clarke says after Calmet that these are simple Israelites, set apart from the priests, Levites and singers already named. Wesley glosses the same phrase as the people of Israel, distinguished from the orders hitherto listed.

debates.question: Is the laity’s roll sound as it stands?

positions.view: No — the sons of Bani are headed twice, and the twenty-seven names following the second heading show a block misfiled under it
Takes the list at face value, marking only the distinction of laity from clergy

outliers.claim: Alone in finding the laity’s roll structurally damaged, and in arguing it from the count of names under each heading rather than from spelling.

of the porters; Shallum, and Telem, and Uri

44.pericope_label: All these had taken strange wives, and some of them had children by them

schools.summary: Gill puts the whole number of offenders at about a hundred and thirteen.

Wesley infers from the notice about children that most of the wives were barren, and reads that barrenness as providence, manifesting God’s displeasure against such matches and keeping the putting away from being encumbered with too many difficulties. He then closes the chapter where its reformers could not: one would think the grievance altogether removed, yet it is met with again in Nehemiah, such corruptions being easily and insensibly brought in though not easily purged out, so that the best reformers can but do their endeavour, and only the Redeemer himself, when he comes to Zion, will effectually turn away ungodliness from Jacob. Clarke draws the opposite emphasis from the same clause, that only a few had children but also that the law was put in execution rigorously, children notwithstanding. He ends on a textual curiosity no other voice raises, reporting from Justin Martyr’s dialogue with Trypho that Ezra offered a paschal lamb on this occasion and addressed the people in words found in no text we have — that this passover is our Savior and our Refuge, that if they would be persuaded of it and humble themselves to him in a sign and afterwards believe in him the place should not be destroyed for ever, but that if they would not believe nor hearken to his preaching they should be a laughing-stock to the Gentiles. Justin’s claim, which Clarke relays without endorsing, is that the Jews blotted the passage out of the book of Ezra from enmity to Christ, and cancelled several other places in the same spirit. Clarke adds the plainer note that in the Hebrew this book and the next make only one, that the Masoretic enumeration of sections treats them as conjoined, and that Nehemiah is nonetheless sometimes distinguished as a second book of Esdras.

debates.question: What does the notice about children imply?

positions.view: That most of the wives were barren, by a providence manifesting displeasure and easing the separation
That only a few had children, and that the law was executed rigorously even so

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting Justin Martyr’s claim that a passage of Ezra about the passover was suppressed out of enmity to Christ.
Alone here in reading the wives’ barrenness as a providence that eased the putting away.

themes: all these had taken strange wives
some of them had wives by whom they had children
